title: Physical contracts: term vs spot, and the key clauses
story: Monday, week four. Lee from the back office drops a thick document on your desk: the contract behind Cargo NS-01. *"Chris agreed the deal on the phone in two minutes. This is what it really says. If the system and the contract do not match, I send the wrong invoice."* Sam adds: *"You do not need to read every page. You need to know which clauses change the money."*
objective: I can explain the difference between a spot and a term contract and name the key clauses that middle office checks.

write.heading: 1. Spot or term?
write.body:
- **Spot contract**: one single delivery, for example one cargo. Cargo NS-01 is a spot deal (→ L20).
- **Term contract**: many deliveries over a long period (for example one cargo per month for a year), at a price formula agreed once.

write.heading: 2. The key clauses
write.body:
| Clause | What it says |
|---|---|
| Quantity | volume and **tolerance** (for example ±5%) |
| Quality | the **specification** of the crude (density, sulphur) |
| Delivery | place, and **laycan**: the window of dates when the ship must arrive |
| Price | a **formula**: benchmark ± differential (→ L8) |
| Payment | when and how (typically about 30 days after loading) |

write.heading: 3. Other important words
write.body:
- **GTCs** (general terms and conditions): standard rules added to the deal, so each contract stays short.
- **Force majeure**: an event outside control (storm, war) that excuses a party.
- **Laytime and demurrage** clauses (→ L19) say who pays if the ship waits.

write.heading: 4. Middle office check
write.body: Example: the contract says 600,000 bbl ±5%, so between 570,000 and 630,000 bbl can be loaded. If 612,000 bbl are loaded, the P&L and the invoice must use 612,000, not 600,000.

check.q: What is the difference between a spot and a term contract?
check.a: A spot contract covers one single delivery (for example one cargo). A term contract covers many deliveries over a long period, at a price formula agreed once.
The window of dates in which the ship must arrive to load. If it comes outside the window, the contract says what happens (for example the buyer can cancel).

check.q: A contract says 600,000 bbl ±5%. What range can be loaded, and which volume goes into the P&L?
check.a: Between 570,000 and 630,000 bbl. The P&L and the invoice use the volume really loaded, not the nominal 600,000 (illustrative numbers).

read_more: In oil, many companies publish their own general terms and conditions (GTCs), and a deal confirmation often just says which GTCs apply, plus the deal-specific terms (quantity, price, dates). In gas and power, European deals are often done under standard master agreements such as the EFET General Agreement; master agreements come back in module 7. The volume really loaded is typically measured at the loading port and written on the **bill of lading**, a key shipping document you will meet soon. The ±5% tolerance, the 30-day payment term and the 612,000 bbl are illustrative; real terms vary from contract to contract. The next lesson explains Incoterms (FOB, CIF, DES): who pays for the ship and when the risk passes from seller to buyer.
